v. 36: “My kingdom is not from this world.”
v. 37: Jesus accepts the title in his own sense: he came to testify to the truth.
¶ The roles are reversed. Pilate thinks he is the judge, but in John’s telling Jesus is the one who questions, and Pilate is the one being judged by the truth.
kw: The Greek word means both the realm and the royal power itself. Jesus speaks of his kingship, his way of being king.
The preposition ek speaks of origin. Jesus does not say his kingdom is absent from this world, but that it does not come from it and does not work by its methods.
In John, truth is not only a correct statement. It is God’s reality made known in Jesus, who says, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (14:6). To belong to the truth is to belong to him.
To bear witness; from this word comes “martyr”. Jesus is King as a witness, and his throne will be the Cross.
vv: Are you the King of the Jews?
In all four Gospels this is Pilate’s first question to Jesus. The same title will be written over the Cross in Hebrew, Latin and Greek (19:19–20).
My kingdom is not from this world. If my kingdom were from this world, my followers would be fighting to keep me from being handed over to the Jews.

Here “the Jews” means the authorities who handed Jesus over, as often in John, not the Jewish people as a whole: Jesus, his mother and his apostles were Jews. The proof that his kingdom is different is simple: no one fights for him. In the garden he told Peter to put away his sword (18:11).
For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.

“Born” and “came into the world” speak of the Incarnation. “Listens to my voice” recalls the Good Shepherd: “My sheep hear my voice” (10:27). The King is the Shepherd, and his subjects are those who listen.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on this verse, notes that Jesus did not say “My kingdom is not here” but “is not from here”: his kingdom is in this world until the end, but it does not take its origin or its strength from the world (in substance). Pope Pius XI instituted the feast of Christ the King in 1925 with the encyclical Quas Primas, for a world that wished to live as if Christ had no claim on society. The Catechism recalls that before Pilate Christ declared that he came to bear witness to the truth (CCC 2471), and that the Church shows forth the kingship of Christ over all creation and in particular over human societies (CCC 2105). The Second Vatican Council describes his kingdom as “a kingdom of truth and life, a kingdom of holiness and grace, a kingdom of justice, love and peace” (Lumen Gentium 36).

qa: Was Melchizedek an appearance of Christ himself?

The Church reads Melchizedek as a real king-priest and a figure of Christ, not Christ himself. When Hebrews says he is “without father, without mother, without genealogy” (7:3), it means that Scripture records none, so that he “resembles the Son of God”. He is a sign that points ahead.
If asking for a king was a rejection of God, why did God allow it?

God respects human choices and works even through poor ones. The monarchy brought many sins, but God made of it the house of David, from which the Messiah was born. This is the pattern of salvation: God draws good out of what we spoil.
Does “my kingdom is not from this world” mean that faith has nothing to say about public life?

No. It means that Christ’s kingdom does not come from worldly power and is not spread by force. But it touches everything: Christians are called to bring the light of Christ into family, work, society and politics, with respect for the conscience of others (CCC 2105; Gaudium et Spes 76).
rite: The Syro-Malabar year closes with the Church looking at her Lord. The weeks of Qudash Edtha have shown the Church as God’s dwelling and as the bride; today she sees her Bridegroom as King. Melchizedek’s bread and wine point to the Holy Qurbana, where the King gives himself as food, and the Rider’s robe dipped in blood points to the Cross, which the East Syriac tradition honours as the sign of victory and of the Lord’s return. Next Sunday the new year opens with Suvara, the season of the Annunciation: the King of kings comes first as a promised child.
study: Abram refused the riches of Sodom but received the blessing of Melchizedek. What offers in my life would make me “rich” at the cost of my faithfulness to God?
In what ways am I tempted, like Israel, to be “like other nations” instead of trusting God’s different way?
The Rider’s weapon is the sword of his mouth. How does the word of God fight the battles of my life?
Jesus says, “Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.” Where do I need to listen to him as my King this week?

lead: Both readings speak of access to the Father. Ephesians says that Christ has broken down the wall between peoples and built them into one house, “a dwelling place for God”. In John, Jesus promises his anxious disciples a place in his Father’s house and calls himself the way to it. The Church, in this season of the Dedication, is the house being built and the road home.

r.h: He is our peace
set: Paul reminds Gentile Christians that they were once “far off”, outside the covenants of Israel, “but now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (2:13). The “dividing wall” recalls the barrier in the Jerusalem Temple that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts; stone notices warning them not to pass it have been found by archaeologists.
str: vv. 14–16: Christ our peace makes the two groups one, through the cross.
vv. 17–18: he proclaimed peace to the far and the near; both have access to the Father in one Spirit.
vv. 19–22: no longer strangers: citizens, household, and a temple built on the apostles and prophets, with Christ as cornerstone.
kw: Not only the end of a quarrel but the Hebrew šālôm: wholeness, right relationship with God and with one another. Paul does not say Christ brings peace, but that he “is” our peace.
The word for being brought into the presence of a king. Through Christ, in the Spirit, every believer may come before the Father.
The stone that holds the whole building together and gives it its line (Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22).
vv: For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
The wall that is broken is the hostility, not Israel’s calling. Paul, a Jew, rejoices that Gentiles now share in Israel’s hope.
for through him both of us have access in one Spirit to the Father.
A small creed of the Trinity: through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father. This is also the shape of Christian prayer.
So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
ch: The Catechism gathers the images of the Church as God’s building, with Christ as the stone rejected by the builders that became the cornerstone, and the Church as the dwelling of God among his people (CCC 756). The Second Vatican Council uses the same images in Lumen Gentium 6. Every church building, consecrated for worship, is a sign of this living temple of people.

r.h: I am the way, and the truth, and the life
set: Jesus speaks at the Last Supper, after Judas has gone out and after he has foretold Peter’s denial (13:30–38). The disciples are afraid: their Master is leaving them. Chapters 14–17 are his farewell words, and they begin with comfort.
str: vv. 1–4: “Do not let your hearts be troubled”: many dwelling places in the Father’s house.
vv. 5–7: Thomas’ question and the answer, “I am the way”.
vv. 8–11: Philip’s request, “show us the Father”.
vv. 12–14: the promise of greater works and of prayer in Jesus’ name.
kw: From menein, to remain, a favourite word of John. It means not passing rooms but places to stay for good. The same word appears in 14:23: the Father and the Son will make their home with the one who loves.
In the Acts of the Apostles the first Christians were called followers of “the Way” (Acts 9:2). Jesus does not only show the way; he is it.
vv: Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”
Thomas asks the honest question many hearts carry, and his question draws out one of the greatest sayings in the Gospel.
I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
Three words, one Person. He is the way because he is the truth about God and gives the life of God.
Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
Jesus is not one more messenger. In his face, words and deeds the Father is made visible.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ’s whole life is a revelation of the Father, and quotes this verse: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (CCC 516). It names Jesus Christ, “the way, and the truth, and the life”, as the first and last point of reference of all Christian teaching on the moral life (CCC 1698). Prayer “in his name” is prayer united to him and to his will (CCC 2614).

qa: If Christ is the only way, what about those who never heard of him?

The Church teaches that all who are saved are saved through Christ, but that God can lead those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel and seek God with a sincere heart (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). Christ remains the way, even for those who do not yet know his name.
rite: For the St Thomas Christians the Gospel has a special note: it is the Apostle Thomas whose question, “How can we know the way?”, draws from the Lord the word “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”. The faith our fathers received from Thomas is faith in this way.
study: Ephesians says Christ “is our peace”. Where is a wall of hostility in my family or parish that he wants to break down?
Thomas was not afraid to ask. What honest question would I like to bring to the Lord in prayer today?

lead: Today’s readings show who belongs to God’s people and how. Peter tells the baptised that they are living stones built into a spiritual house, “a royal priesthood”. In John, Jesus is the gate of the sheepfold and the good shepherd who lays down his life and gathers “one flock”. The Church is both a house of living stones and a flock gathered by one Shepherd.

r.h: Living stones, a royal priesthood
set: The letter is addressed “to the exiles of the Dispersion” in five regions of Asia Minor (1:1): Christians, mostly of Gentile background, who felt like strangers in their own towns. Much of its language is baptismal. Having been “born anew” (1:23), they are now told what they have become.
str: vv. 1–3: put away malice; long for the pure spiritual milk like newborn infants.
vv. 4–8: come to Christ, the living stone, and be built into a spiritual house; three Old Testament texts about the stone.
vv. 9–10: the titles of God’s people, taken from Exodus 19:6, Isaiah 43:20–21 and Hosea.
kw: A paradox: stones are dead things. Christ is the stone that was rejected and is now risen and living; joined to him, believers become living stones too.
From the Greek of Exodus 19:6. The whole people shares in Christ’s priesthood, offering “spiritual sacrifices”, that is, lives given to God in the Spirit.
vv: Like newborn infants, long for the pure, spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow into salvation
An image for the newly baptised. The milk is the word of God and the grace of Christ; the verb “long for” describes a hungry baby’s cry.
like living stones, let yourselves be built into a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people, in order that you may proclaim the mighty acts of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.
The titles of Israel at Sinai are now given to the Church, not to replace Israel but to share in her calling. The purpose is mission: to proclaim God’s mighty acts.
ch: The Catechism applies this passage to baptism: the baptised “have become ‘living stones’ to be ‘built into a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood’” (CCC 1268). The whole community of believers is priestly, sharing in Christ’s priesthood by baptism, while the ministerial priesthood serves this common priesthood (CCC 1546–1547; Lumen Gentium 10).

r.h: One flock, one shepherd
set: Jesus speaks after healing the man born blind, whom some leaders had driven out (John 9). His words recall Ezekiel 34, where God condemns the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises, “I myself will search for my sheep” (34:11).
str: vv. 7–10: “I am the gate”: whoever enters by him will find pasture and abundant life.
vv. 11–13: “I am the good shepherd”, contrasted with the hired hand.
vv. 14–16: mutual knowledge, the shepherd’s life laid down, and the other sheep to be gathered.
kw: The door of the fold. Jesus is the only rightful way in for the sheep and for those who would shepherd them.
More than morally good: noble, beautiful, true. He is the real shepherd, the one a shepherd is meant to be.
One who works for pay and has no bond with the sheep. When danger comes, he thinks of himself.
vv: I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly.
The purpose of Jesus’ coming in one line. “Life” in John is the life of God himself, given now and lasting for ever.
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
Said several times in this chapter in different forms (10:11, 15, 17–18). Ordinary shepherds risked their lives; this Shepherd gives his.
I have other sheep that do not belong to this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd.
The other sheep are the Gentiles who will come to faith. Unity is the Shepherd’s work and his desire.
ch: The Catechism says that the Church is a sheepfold whose one and necessary door is Christ, and a flock of which God himself foretold that he would be the shepherd (CCC 754). St Augustine, preaching on this chapter, notes that Christ is both the door and the shepherd: he enters by himself (in substance). The words “one flock, one shepherd” stand behind the Church’s prayer and work for the unity of all Christians (Unitatis Redintegratio 1–2).

qa: What does “a royal priesthood” mean if we also have ordained priests?

All the baptised share in Christ’s priesthood by offering their lives, prayers and work to God. Ordained priests receive a different sacramental ministry to serve this priestly people in Christ’s name, above all in the Holy Qurbana. The two are related but differ in essence, not only in degree (Lumen Gentium 10).
study: Peter calls Christians “living stones”. What does it mean for me to let myself be built into the parish community rather than stand apart?
Who are the “other sheep” in my surroundings that the Shepherd wants to gather, and how can I help?

lead: Two hymns of praise stand side by side today. Ephesians opens with a great blessing of God for his plan, chosen “before the foundation of the world” and fulfilled in Christ. Luke gives us the Magnificat, Mary’s song for what God has done for her and for his people. One hymn looks at God’s plan from eternity; the other sees it come true in a humble young woman of Nazareth.

r.h: Blessed be the God and Father
set: In Greek, verses 3–14 form one single long sentence, a hymn that seems to run out of breath in praise. It takes the form of the Jewish berakah, a prayer that begins “Blessed be God” and then lists his works. Paul blesses the Father for what he has done in Christ, and the passage moves from eternity (v. 4) to the fullness of time (v. 10).
str: v. 3: the blessing of the Father for every spiritual blessing in Christ.
vv. 4–6: chosen and destined to be his adopted children.
vv. 7–8: redemption through his blood and forgiveness.
vv. 9–10: the mystery of his will: to gather up all things in Christ.
vv. 11–12: our inheritance, so that we may live for the praise of his glory.
kw: God blesses us with gifts; we bless God with praise. The same word goes down and comes back up.
Literally “to bring under one head”. St Irenaeus built his teaching of “recapitulation” on this word: Christ takes up the whole story of humanity and of creation and heals it in himself.
Not a riddle but God’s hidden plan, now revealed. The Syriac tradition speaks of raza, the mystery made present in the liturgy.
vv: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places,
just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.
Before anything existed, God thought of us in his Son. The aim of the choice is holiness, and its atmosphere is love.
as a plan for the fullness of time, to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.
The whole universe has one centre and one goal: Christ.
ch: The Catechism opens its teaching on the liturgy with this hymn: in the liturgy the Father is blessed as the source of every blessing (CCC 1077–1078). It also calls God’s plan, revealed in Ephesians 1, a “plan of loving kindness” conceived before the creation of the world (CCC 257).

r.h: My soul magnifies the Lord
set: Mary has gone in haste to visit Elizabeth, and Elizabeth has called her “blessed” (1:42–45). Mary answers not by speaking about herself but by praising God. Her song is woven from Old Testament texts, above all the song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2:1–10), another woman whose child was God’s gift.
str: vv. 46–50: what God has done for Mary.
vv. 51–53: what God does in the world: the proud scattered, the lowly lifted up.
vv. 54–55: what God has done for Israel, faithful to his promise to Abraham.
kw: To make great, to declare great. Mary cannot make God greater, but she makes his greatness known.
Low estate, humble condition. It is not first a virtue Mary claims but the smallness God chose to look upon.
In the Greek Old Testament it often renders the Hebrew ḥesed, God’s faithful covenant love. The word appears at the centre (v. 50) and the end (v. 54) of the song.
vv: for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant. Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed;
A prophecy fulfilled every time the Church honours Mary. Her blessedness comes from God’s look, not from her own greatness.
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly;
The verbs are in the past tense, as if God’s reversal were already done. In Christ it has begun.
according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever.
The song ends with Abraham. What God is doing in Mary is the fulfilment of a very old promise.
ch: The Catechism calls the Magnificat “the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church” (CCC 2619). St Ambrose, commenting on this Gospel, wishes that the soul of Mary be in each of us to magnify the Lord, and her spirit in each of us to rejoice in God (in substance).

qa: Did Mary really compose such a hymn?

Mary was a young Jewish woman whose prayer was formed by the psalms and the songs of Scripture. The Magnificat is built from those texts, as a devout person of her time could pray. A few old Latin manuscripts attribute the song to Elizabeth, but almost all manuscripts and the whole tradition of the Church give it to Mary.
study: Ephesians says God chose me “before the foundation of the world”. How would my day change if I truly believed this?
Mary praises God for looking on her lowliness. Where in my life do I need to let God look on my smallness rather than hide it?

lead: Both readings lift our eyes beyond this world. Hebrews reminds Christians that “here we have no lasting city” and calls them to go out to Christ and offer a sacrifice of praise. In Luke the seventy return rejoicing in their power over demons, and Jesus tells them to rejoice rather that their names are written in heaven. Our true home and our true joy are with God.

r.h: Here we have no lasting city
set: These are some of the closing exhortations of Hebrews. The readers were being drawn by “strange teachings”, perhaps about sacred meals and food laws. The author answers with the image of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16): the bodies of the animals whose blood was carried into the sanctuary were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27).
str: vv. 9–10: hearts strengthened by grace, not by food; “we have an altar”.
vv. 11–12: the sin offering burned outside the camp, and Jesus who suffered outside the city gate.
vv. 13–14: “let us then go to him outside the camp”, seeking the city to come.
vv. 15–16: the sacrifice of praise, and the sacrifices of doing good and sharing.
kw: The author does not explain which altar he means. Many see the Cross; Catholic tradition also sees the Eucharistic table, where the one sacrifice of the Cross is made present.
In the Greek Old Testament this renders the tôdâ, the thanksgiving offering. Christian worship is a thanksgiving offered through Christ.
The word behind “to share what you have” (v. 16). Communion with God is lived out in sharing with others.
vv: We have an altar from which those who officiate in the tent have no right to eat.
Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood.
Golgotha lay outside the walls of Jerusalem (John 19:17, 20). The place of shame becomes the place of holiness.
For here we have no lasting city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.
Christians are pilgrims. This does not make them careless about the earthly city; it breaks the hold of its idols on them.
Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
Worship and charity belong together: praise on the lips and bread shared with the poor.
ch: The Catechism lists “the sacrifice of praise” among the names of the Eucharist (CCC 1330). The early Letter to Diognetus describes Christians as living in their own countries as sojourners, for whom every foreign land is a homeland and every homeland a foreign land (in substance).

r.h: Rejoice that your names are written in heaven
set: Luke alone tells of a second, larger mission: Jesus sends disciples ahead of him in pairs (10:1–12). Now they return with joy. The mission of these disciples anticipates the mission of the Church to all nations.
str: v. 17: the joyful report: “even the demons submit to us”.
vv. 18–19: Jesus’ vision of Satan’s fall and the authority he gives.
v. 20: the deeper reason for joy.
v. 21: Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit and praises the Father.
kw: The image of the book of life (Exodus 32:32; Daniel 12:1; Philippians 4:3). To be written there is to belong to God for ever.
A word of exultant joy, used in Mary’s “my spirit rejoices” (1:47). Here Jesus rejoices “in the Holy Spirit”: Father, Son and Spirit appear together.
Little children, the simple. God reveals himself to those who receive him as a gift.
vv: The seventy returned with joy, saying, “Lord, in your name even the demons submit to us!”

A note on the text. The ancient manuscripts differ here and in 10:1. Some important ones read “seventy” (followed by the NRSV), others, also very old, read “seventy-two” (followed by the Malayalam POC). The numbers may recall the table of the nations in Genesis 10, which counts seventy nations in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Either way, the mission points to the whole world.
I watched Satan fall from heaven like a flash of lightning.
The mission of the disciples is part of the defeat of evil. Satan’s power is already broken.
but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.
Success in ministry is a gift, but it is not the deepest joy. The deepest joy is to be known and loved by God.
ch: The Catechism presents this moment as a model of Jesus’ prayer: his thanksgiving to the Father, Lord of heaven and earth, for revealing the mysteries of the Kingdom to little ones (CCC 2603). The Kingdom belongs to the poor and the lowly, who receive it with humble hearts (CCC 544).

study: Hebrews says, “here we have no lasting city.” What attachment in my life makes me forget that I am a pilgrim?
Do I rejoice more in what I achieve for God or in the fact that my name is written in heaven?

lead: As the liturgical year draws to its close, both readings look at the life beyond death. Revelation shows a great multitude from every nation worshipping before the throne and the Lamb. In Mark, Jesus answers those who deny the resurrection: God “is God not of the dead, but of the living”. The Church on earth already sings with the Church in heaven.

r.h: A great multitude that no one could count
set: Chapter 6 ends with a terrified question: when God’s judgment comes, “who is able to stand?” (6:17). Chapter 7 is the answer. First John hears the number of those sealed from the twelve tribes of Israel, 144,000 (7:4–8), a number of fullness. Then he looks and sees a crowd beyond counting, from all nations. The people of God is complete, and it is universal.
str: v. 9: the multitude from every nation, robed in white, with palm branches.
v. 10: their cry: salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb.
vv. 11–12: angels, elders and living creatures fall down and worship with a sevenfold blessing.
kw: Palms were carried at the feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40) and greeted Jesus at his entry into Jerusalem (John 12:13). They are signs of victory and joy.
The elder explains that they “have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (7:14). Their purity is a gift won by Christ.
They do not say that they have won, but that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb.
vv: After this I looked, and there was a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, robed in white, with palm branches in their hands.
God’s promise to Abraham of descendants as many as the stars (Genesis 15:5) comes true here, in every language.
Salvation belongs to our God who is seated on the throne, and to the Lamb!
Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen.
Seven words of praise, the number of fullness, framed by two Amens. Heaven is a liturgy.
ch: The Catechism lists those who take part in the heavenly liturgy described in Revelation, ending with “a great multitude which no one could number, from every nation” (CCC 1138). The Second Vatican Council teaches that in the liturgy we are united with the Church in heaven and join in its praise (Lumen Gentium 50).

r.h: God not of the dead, but of the living
set: Jesus is in the Temple in Jerusalem in his last days, and various groups come to test him (11:27–12:37). The Sadducees were a priestly party linked to the Temple leadership. They rejected the oral traditions of the Pharisees and, as Mark says, denied the resurrection (see also Acts 23:8).

Their question rests on the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10): if a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow so that the dead man’s name would not be lost. They build an absurd case to make belief in the resurrection look foolish.
str: vv. 18–23: the Sadducees’ case of the seven brothers.
vv. 24–25: first answer: they do not know the power of God; the risen life is not a copy of this one.
vv. 26–27: second answer from the Scriptures: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
kw: Literally “standing up again”. Jesus speaks of a real rising of the whole person, not only the survival of a shadow.
From the verb “to wander, to go astray”, said twice (vv. 24, 27). The Sadducees have lost their way because they know neither the Scriptures nor God’s power.
vv: Is not this the reason you are wrong, that you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God?
For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
“Like” angels, not turned into angels. Marriage belongs to this age, where life must be handed on; in the resurrection, death is no more and all love is taken up into God.
He is God not of the dead, but of the living; you are quite wrong.
God spoke to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:6) long after the patriarchs had died, and still called himself their God. A covenant with God is not broken by death.
ch: The Catechism quotes Jesus’ answer to the Sadducees as his firm teaching on the resurrection, and links faith in the resurrection to faith in God the Creator (CCC 993). Heaven is perfect life and communion of love with the Holy Trinity, the Virgin Mary, the angels and all the blessed (CCC 1024).

qa: Will husbands and wives know each other in heaven?

Jesus does not say that love ends, but that marriage as a way of handing on life belongs to this world. The Church teaches that in heaven all true love is purified and fulfilled in the communion of saints (CCC 1024). Those who loved each other in God will not be strangers there.
study: The multitude in Revelation comes from every nation and language. How does my parish show that the Church is meant for all peoples?
Jesus says the Sadducees know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Which of the two do I most need to grow in?

lead: On the last Saturday of Qudash Edtha the Church keeps the feast of St Andrew the Apostle, and the readings follow the path of a call. Jacob, a fugitive, sees a ladder joining earth to heaven and says, “this is the gate of heaven”. Zechariah sees people of every language take hold of a Jew’s garment and say, “Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.” Paul asks how anyone can believe unless someone is sent to proclaim. In Matthew, Jesus walks by the lake and calls Andrew and his brother: “Follow me.” Andrew, the first to follow and the one who brought others to Jesus, stands where these lines meet.

r.h: Surely the Lord is in this place
set: Jacob has taken the blessing meant for his brother Esau by deceit (Genesis 27), and now he flees from Esau’s anger toward Haran, to his mother’s family. He is alone, at night, with a stone for a pillow. At this low point God meets him for the first time.
The place will be called Bethel, “house of God” (28:19). It later became one of Israel’s great sanctuaries.
str: vv. 10–11: the journey, the sunset, the stone.
v. 12: the dream: a ladder, its top reaching to heaven, angels going up and down.
vv. 13–15: the Lord’s promise: the land, descendants, blessing for all families, and “I am with you”.
vv. 16–17: Jacob awakes in awe: “the house of God … the gate of heaven”.
kw: The word appears only here in the Bible. It may mean a stairway or ramp, like the steps of the temple towers of Mesopotamia. Unlike them, this stairway is not built by men to reach heaven (compare Babel, Genesis 11:4); it comes down from God.

The Hebrew of v. 13 can mean “beside him” (Jacob) or “above it” (the ladder). The NRSV chooses “beside him”, the Malayalam POC “at the top of the ladder”. Both are possible, and both are true: God is above all, and near.
A gate is where one passes from outside to inside. Jacob discovers that heaven has an entrance on earth, where God chooses to meet us.
vv: And he dreamed that there was a ladder set up on the earth, the top of it reaching to heaven; and the angels of God were ascending and descending on it.
The angels go up first, then down. Communion between heaven and earth already exists; Jacob is allowed to see it.
Know that I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land; for I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.
God makes this promise to a man who has just deceived his father and brother. Grace comes before Jacob deserves it, and it will change him.
Surely the Lord is in this place … and I did not know it!
How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
These words are sung at the dedication of churches in many liturgical traditions. Every consecrated church is a Bethel.
ch: Jesus himself gives the key to this passage. To Nathanael, in the chapter where Andrew first follows him, he says, “you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:51). Christ is the true ladder, the meeting place of heaven and earth. Many Fathers developed this reading, and the Eastern hymn tradition also greets Mary as the heavenly ladder by which God came down, since through her the Son became man.

r.h: Let us go with you, for God is with you
set: Zechariah prophesied in 520–518 BC, when the exiles who had returned from Babylon were rebuilding the Temple in a poor and ruined Jerusalem (Zechariah 1:1; Ezra 5:1). Chapter 8 is a series of short promises, each beginning “Thus says the Lord of hosts”. Today’s passage is the last and greatest: the nations themselves will come to seek the Lord.
str: vv. 20–21: peoples of many cities encourage one another: “Come, let us go”.
v. 22: many peoples and strong nations come to Jerusalem to seek the Lord.
v. 23: ten men from every language take hold of the garment of one Jew.
kw: The Lord of the heavenly armies, the King of all. The title is used again and again in Zechariah 8.
entreat the favour of the Lord
Literally “to soften the face of the Lord”: to seek his kindness in prayer.
The corner or fringe of a garment, where a devout Israelite wore the tassels commanded in Numbers 15:38. To grasp it is to cling to someone as a guide.
vv: Come, let us go to entreat the favor of the Lord, and to seek the Lord of hosts; I myself am going.
Faith spreads from city to city, from neighbour to neighbour. The last words, “I myself am going”, show that the one who invites also goes.
In those days ten men from nations of every language shall take hold of a Jew, grasping his garment and saying, “Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.”
Ten is a round number of fullness. One faithful person becomes the way by which many come to God.
ch: Jesus said to the Samaritan woman that “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22). The Church gratefully acknowledges that she received the revelation of the Old Testament through the people of Israel and draws nourishment from that root (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). The scene of Zechariah is lived again when Greeks come to Philip and say, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus”, and Philip goes with Andrew to tell Jesus (John 12:20–22).

r.h: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news
set: In Romans 9–11 Paul wrestles with a painful question: why has much of his own people, Israel, not accepted Jesus as Messiah? In chapter 10 he explains that the righteousness of faith is near, “on your lips and in your heart” (10:8, from Deuteronomy 30:14). Then he shows how faith comes to anyone: through a chain that begins with God sending messengers.
str: vv. 9–10: confess with the lips, believe in the heart.
vv. 11–13: no distinction between Jew and Greek; everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.
vv. 14–15: the chain: call, believe, hear, proclaim, be sent.
vv. 16–18: not all have obeyed; yet the voice has gone out to all the earth.
kw: One of the oldest Christian confessions of faith. In the Greek Old Testament “Lord” (Kyrios) stands for the divine name; to call Jesus Lord is to confess his divinity.
From this verb comes “apostle”, one who is sent. No one can make himself a messenger; he must be sent.
Faith comes from hearing. The Christian faith is received, not invented.
vv: because if you confess with your lips that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
Lips and heart, outward and inward. Faith that is real is spoken, and words that are true come from the heart.
And how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”
Isaiah 52:7 speaks of the messenger running over the mountains to Jerusalem with news of peace. The feet are dusty and tired, but beautiful because of the news they carry.
So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.
Paul applies to the preachers of the Gospel the words of Psalm 19:4 about the heavens declaring God’s glory. The Church has long sung this verse on the feasts of apostles.
ch: The Catechism quotes this chain of questions to show that no one can give himself the mandate to preach the Gospel: the ministers of the Church are sent by Christ (CCC 875). It recalls that the earliest Christian confession, “Jesus is Lord”, attributes to Jesus the divine sovereignty (CCC 449). The Church is missionary by her very nature (Ad Gentes 2).

r.h: Follow me, and I will make you fish for people
set: After John the Baptist is arrested, Jesus leaves Nazareth and settles in Capernaum by the Sea of Galilee, and begins to preach: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near” (4:12–17). His first act is to call companions.

Fishing was the main trade of the lake towns. A man standing in the shallows would throw a round casting net; others worked from boats with larger nets, which needed constant mending. Andrew, whose name is Greek and means “manly”, came from Bethsaida (John 1:44). John’s Gospel tells that he was first a disciple of John the Baptist and had already met Jesus, and that he brought his brother Simon to him (John 1:35–42).
str: v. 18: Jesus sees Simon and Andrew casting a net.
v. 19: the call and the promise.
v. 20: they leave their nets immediately.
vv. 21–22: the call of James and John, who leave the boat and their father.
kw: Literally “Come after me”. Rabbis did not usually call their pupils; pupils chose a teacher. Here Jesus takes the initiative.
Their old skill is taken up into a new mission. The prophets had used the image of fishers gathering people (Jeremiah 16:16).
Said of both pairs of brothers. The call of Jesus has an authority that makes a quick and whole answer possible.
vv: As he walked by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea
Jesus sees them at their ordinary work. God’s call usually comes in the middle of daily life.
And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.”
Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
The nets were their living. To leave them is to trust that the one who calls will provide.
ch: The Catechism teaches that from the beginning Jesus associated his disciples with his own life and mission (CCC 787). The Byzantine tradition honours Andrew as the “First-called” (Prōtoklētos), because in John’s Gospel he was the first to follow Jesus and at once brought his brother to him. Tradition holds that he preached in the regions around the Black Sea and in Greece, and was martyred at Patras in Achaia; later tradition says on a cross shaped like an X. He is the patron of the Church of Constantinople, and each year on his feast a delegation of the Holy See visits the Ecumenical Patriarch, as a sign of the brotherhood of the Churches of Peter and of Andrew.

qa: Why did Andrew and Peter follow Jesus so quickly?

Matthew stresses the power of Jesus’ word. John’s Gospel adds that Andrew had already met Jesus and spent a day with him, and had told Peter, “We have found the Messiah” (John 1:41). Both are true: the call by the lake came to men whose hearts had already been touched.
Is it enough to say “Jesus is Lord” to be saved?

Paul means a confession that comes from a heart that believes, the faith of the whole person. Elsewhere he speaks of “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). Saying the words without living them is not what he means; living faith includes both the confession and a life that follows.
Was Jacob’s ladder a real ladder?

The Hebrew word probably means a stairway. It was a dream, a vision given by God. Its truth is in its meaning: heaven is not closed, God comes down to meet us, and in Christ the way between heaven and earth stays open.
rite: Andrew and Thomas were brothers in the one apostolic college, and the Syro-Malabar Church, founded on the preaching of St Thomas, honours Andrew as the one who first brought others to Jesus. On this last Saturday of the Dedication season the words of Jacob fit our churches: each is “the house of God” and “the gate of heaven”, where in the Holy Qurbana heaven is opened. Andrew’s first act after meeting Jesus was to find his brother; every Christian family and parish is called to do the same.
study: Jacob said, “Surely the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.” Where has God been present in my life when I did not recognise him?
Zechariah sees people saying, “Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.” Can people see in me that God is with me?
Paul asks, “How are they to hear without someone to proclaim him?” To whom am I being sent?
Andrew left his nets. What “nets” keep me from following Jesus more closely?

lead: A new liturgical year begins with Suvara, the season of the Annunciation, and its first Sunday is full of announcements. God tells Abraham that Sarah, at ninety, will bear a son. Isaiah hears God say to his people in exile, “I have called you by name, you are mine.” In the Temple, Gabriel tells the old priest Zechariah that Elizabeth will bear John. Between these births stands Ephesians, which speaks of the family as the place where Christ’s love is lived. The East Syriac year begins not with a command but with a promise: God comes to barren places and makes them fruitful.

r.h: Sarah shall be her name
set: Abram is ninety-nine years old. God appears to him, makes an everlasting covenant, changes his name to Abraham, “father of a multitude”, and gives circumcision as its sign (17:1–14). Today’s passage continues the same speech: now God turns to Sarai.
Abraham already has a son, Ishmael, born of Hagar (Genesis 16). It seems natural to him that the promise should pass through Ishmael. God has another plan.
str: vv. 15–16: Sarai’s new name and the promise of a son through her.
v. 17: Abraham falls on his face and laughs.
v. 18: his prayer for Ishmael.
vv. 19–21: God’s answer: a son named Isaac, the covenant with him; a blessing also for Ishmael.
v. 22: God goes up from Abraham.
kw: Both Sarai and Sarah are forms meaning “princess”. The new name marks a new mission: “kings of peoples shall come from her” (17:16).
The name means “he laughs” or “may God laugh”. Abraham laughs here, Sarah will laugh in 18:12, and at the birth Sarah says, “God has brought laughter for me” (21:6). Doubt becomes joy.
A covenant that does not end. God binds himself to Abraham’s descendants for ever.
vv: Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed, and said to himself, “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Can Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?”
He bows in worship and laughs in disbelief at the same time. Scripture does not hide the struggle of the father of faith.
O that Ishmael might live in your sight!
As for Ishmael, I have heard you; I will bless him and make him fruitful and exceedingly numerous; he shall be the father of twelve princes, and I will make him a great nation.
God hears the father’s prayer. Ishmael is not rejected; he receives his own blessing, fulfilled in Genesis 25:12–16.
But my covenant I will establish with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this season next year.
The promise is given a date. God’s word enters time and history.
ch: St Paul presents Abraham as the model of faith who “did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was already as good as dead” (Romans 4:19). The Catechism calls Abraham the model of obedience in faith, and Sarah the one who conceived the son of the promise (CCC 144–146). The birth of a son from a barren mother by God’s power prepares the births of John and of Jesus, where the angel says, “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37; compare Genesis 18:14).

r.h: I have called you by name, you are mine
set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the Jews in exile in Babylon in the sixth century BC. They are discouraged and feel abandoned. The prophet brings words of comfort: the God who created Israel will redeem them and bring them home. The lectionary adds vv. 10–11, where Israel is called to be God’s witness.
str: v. 1: “Do not fear”: God creates, redeems and calls by name.
v. 2: through waters and fire, God is with them.
vv. 3–4: “you are precious in my sight”: the ransom.
vv. 5–7: the gathering of sons and daughters from the ends of the earth.
vv. 10–11: “You are my witnesses”; “besides me there is no savior”.
kw: The gō’ēl was the next of kin who bought back a relative from slavery or recovered his land. God acts as Israel’s nearest kinsman.
The price paid for a life. The language is poetic: God values Israel more than great nations.
In a court scene, the nations’ gods cannot produce witnesses; Israel’s very existence is God’s testimony.
vv: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.
To be called by name is to be known personally. These words are often read at baptisms: each child is called by name and belongs to God.
When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you
The waters recall the Red Sea and the Jordan. God does not promise a life without waters and fire, but his presence in them.
Because you are precious in my sight, and honored, and I love you
You are my witnesses, says the Lord, and my servant whom I have chosen, so that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he.
“I am he” (’ănî hû’) echoes the divine name. Jesus will use the same words: “then you will realize that I am he” (John 8:28).
ch: The Catechism teaches that God calls each one by name, that everyone’s name is sacred, and that the name is given in baptism (CCC 2156–2158). Isaiah’s words show that this is not a formality: the God who made the stars calls each person as his own.

r.h: Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ
set: Ephesians 5:21–6:9 is a “household code”, a common form in the ancient world that set out duties within the family: husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and slaves. Similar lists appear in Colossians 3:18–4:1 and 1 Peter 2–3. Paul uses the familiar form but transforms it from within: everything is placed under Christ, and the first word is mutual submission.
str: 5:21: the principle for all: be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ.
5:22–24: wives and husbands, as the Church and Christ.
5:25–30: husbands are to love as Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her.
5:31–33: “the two will become one flesh”: a great mystery about Christ and the Church.
6:1–4: children and parents.
kw: The participle governs the whole passage. No one stands outside this mutual service; it is the attitude of all who fear Christ.
The husband’s duty is not to rule but to love with the love of Christ, a love measured by the Cross: he “gave himself up for her”.
The Latin Vulgate translated this as sacramentum hoc magnum est. The union of husband and wife reflects the union of Christ and the Church.
vv: Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ.
This verse is the key that opens the rest. Whatever is said to wives, husbands, children and fathers is said within mutual submission.
Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,
In the ancient world this was the startling part. The husband is given the hardest command: to lay down his life.
This is a great mystery, and I am applying it to Christ and the church.
And, fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
Parental authority is also service. Fathers are to form their children patiently in the Lord, not crush them.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage to show that “the entire Christian life bears the mark of the spousal love of Christ and the Church”, and that Christian marriage is an efficacious sign of the covenant between Christ and the Church (CCC 1616–1617). The family is “the domestic church” (CCC 1656; Lumen Gentium 11). St John Paul II taught that the “mutual subjection out of reverence for Christ” of 5:21 is the Gospel’s newness in this passage: the subjection is not one-sided but mutual (Mulieris Dignitatem 24, in substance).

r.h: Your prayer has been heard
set: After a short preface (1:1–4), Luke opens his Gospel in the Temple of Jerusalem, where it will also end (24:53). He builds the first chapter as a diptych: the announcement of John’s birth and the announcement of Jesus’ birth, side by side, so that John always points to someone greater.

Background: the priests were divided into twenty-four divisions, each serving in the Temple for a week twice a year; Abijah was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:10). There were so many priests that the privilege of offering incense in the Holy Place, chosen by lot, might come only once in a lifetime. Incense was offered at the morning and evening sacrifice, while the people prayed outside.
str: vv. 5–7: Zechariah and Elizabeth: righteous, blameless, and childless.
vv. 8–10: the lot, the incense, the people praying outside.
vv. 11–17: the angel’s appearance and message about John.
vv. 18–20: Zechariah’s doubt and the sign of silence.
vv. 21–23: he comes out unable to speak.
vv. 24–25: Elizabeth conceives and praises God.
kw: A personal petition. “Your prayer has been heard” may refer both to the couple’s long prayer for a child and to the priest’s prayer for Israel’s redemption.
The name means “the Lord has been gracious”. Zechariah means “the Lord has remembered”. The names tell the story: God remembers and shows grace.
“God is my strength” or “mighty one of God”. He appeared to Daniel “at the time of the evening sacrifice” (Daniel 9:21); now he comes again at the hour of the incense offering.
vv: Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you will name him John.
The first words of the Gospel’s first angel are “Do not be afraid”. They will be heard again by Mary (1:30) and by the shepherds (2:10).
With the spirit and power of Elijah he will go before him, to turn the hearts of parents to their children
The angel quotes Malachi 4:5–6, the last words of the prophets in the Christian Old Testament. The long silence of prophecy is about to end.
But now, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time, you will become mute, unable to speak, until the day these things occur.
The silence is both a sign and a discipline. The priest who could not believe must now listen. When he speaks again, it will be to bless God (1:64).
This is what the Lord has done for me when he looked favorably on me and took away the disgrace I have endured among my people.
Elizabeth’s words anticipate Mary’s: God “has looked with favor” (1:48).
ch: The Catechism teaches that John was “filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb”, and that he is the Elijah who was to come, sent to “make ready a people prepared for the Lord” (CCC 717–718). St Ambrose, commenting on Luke, notes that Zechariah lost his voice through doubt and recovered it through faith when he named his son (in substance).

qa: Why was Zechariah punished for his question when Mary was not?

Zechariah asked for proof: “How will I know that this is so?” (1:18). Mary asked how it would happen, since she was a virgin (1:34), and then gave her full consent (1:38). The Fathers saw in Zechariah a doubt about God’s word, and in Mary a faith that seeks understanding. Even so, his silence was a mercy that prepared him to praise.
Does Ephesians 5 make wives inferior to husbands?

No. The passage begins with mutual submission (5:21), and it asks of husbands the self-giving love of Christ on the Cross. Paul speaks in the language of his time, but he fills it with a new spirit. The Church teaches the equal dignity of man and woman (CCC 369–372; Mulieris Dignitatem 24).
What does the Church say about Ishmael?

Genesis shows God hearing Abraham’s prayer and blessing Ishmael. The Church regards with esteem the Muslims, who link their faith to Abraham (Nostra Aetate 3). The covenant line passes through Isaac, but God’s care reaches Ishmael too.
rite: In the East Syriac tradition the liturgical year begins with Suvara, the Annunciation, rather than with the end of the world. The Syro-Malabar Church starts the year by listening to God’s promises: to Abraham, to Zechariah and, in the coming weeks, to Mary and Joseph. Zechariah offering incense in the sanctuary while the people pray outside is close to our own experience: in the Holy Qurbana the priest stands at the altar in the sanctuary on behalf of the people, and the prayers of all rise together like incense. Suvara is also a season for families, and today’s epistle invites every home to become a place where God’s announcements are heard.
study: Abraham laughed at God’s promise, and later Sarah laughed with joy. What promise of God do I find hard to believe?
God says, “I have called you by name, you are mine.” How can I help a child or a young person in my family to know this?
Ephesians begins with “Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ.” What would mutual submission look like in my home this week?
Zechariah was silent for months and then spoke to bless God. What might God want to teach me through silence in this season of Suvara?

lead: On the first weekday of Suvara both readings speak of faith. Paul tells the Galatians that the blessing of Abraham comes through faith, and that Christ took the curse upon himself so that the blessing might reach all nations. In Luke, the disciples cannot heal a suffering boy, and Jesus laments a “faithless and perverse generation” before he heals him. Faith is not our achievement; it is trust in the One who can do what we cannot.

r.h: The righteous will live by faith
set: Some teachers were telling the Gentile Christians of Galatia that they had to be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses to belong fully to God’s people. Paul answers from the story of Abraham, who “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (3:6; Genesis 15:6) long before the Law was given. Paul uses four Old Testament texts: Deuteronomy 27:26, Habakkuk 2:4, Leviticus 18:5 and Deuteronomy 21:23.
str: v. 9: those who believe are blessed with Abraham.
vv. 10–12: relying on the works of the Law brings a curse, because no one keeps it all; the righteous live by faith.
vv. 13–14: Christ became a curse for us so that Abraham’s blessing might come to the Gentiles and we might receive the Spirit.
kw: The opposite of blessing. In Deuteronomy, blessing and curse are set before Israel (Deuteronomy 27–28). Paul shows Christ taking the curse so that the blessing may flow.
To buy out of the market, as a slave was bought and released. The price was Christ’s own life.
In Habakkuk 2:4 the Hebrew word means steadfast faithfulness and trust. Paul reads it as the faith by which a person rests on God.
vv: For this reason, those who believe are blessed with Abraham who believed.
Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law; for “The one who is righteous will live by faith.”
Habakkuk spoke in a time of crisis: the righteous will survive by holding fast to God. Paul sees here the whole of the Gospel.
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us
Deuteronomy 21:23 said that one hung on a tree was under God’s curse. The crucified Christ entered that place of shame for our sake. This is exchange: he took our curse, we receive his blessing.
in order that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.
ch: The Council of Trent teaches that faith is “the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification” (Session VI, chapter 8), and the Catechism teaches that justification is the gift of God’s grace received in faith and baptism (CCC 1987–1992). Paul himself says that what counts is “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, expressing a common understanding of these basic truths.

r.h: All were astounded at the greatness of God
set: The day before, Jesus had been transfigured on the mountain before Peter, John and James (9:28–36). Now he comes down to a crowd and a crisis. The other disciples had been given “power and authority over all demons” (9:1), but they could not cure this boy. Mark’s account adds that “This kind can come out only through prayer” (Mark 9:29).
str: v. 37: the descent from the mountain; a great crowd.
vv. 38–40: the father’s plea: his only child, and the disciples’ failure.
v. 41: Jesus’ lament: “You faithless and perverse generation”.
vv. 42–43a: the healing, and the amazement at the greatness of God.
kw: Luke alone notes that the child was an only son, as he does for the widow’s son at Nain (7:12) and Jairus’ daughter (8:42). The pain of a parent is close to Jesus’ heart.
An echo of Moses’ song, “a perverse and crooked generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5). The lament is for the whole age, the disciples included, not for the father only.
The same word is used in 2 Peter 1:16 for the Transfiguration: “we had been eyewitnesses of his majesty”. The glory seen on the mountain is now seen in the valley, in an act of mercy.
vv: Teacher, I beg you to look at my son; he is my only child.
A father’s prayer, simple and direct: “look at my son”. He asks first for Jesus’ attention.
You faithless and perverse generation, how much longer must I be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.
The lament ends with a command of hope: “Bring your son here.” Jesus’ patience is greater than our lack of faith.
But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.
“Gave him back to his father”: as with the widow of Nain (7:15), Jesus restores the family, not only the sick person.
And all were astounded at the greatness of God.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ exorcisms release people from the domination of demons and anticipate his great victory over “the ruler of this world” (CCC 550). It also distinguishes clearly between possession and illness: psychological illness is a very different matter, and treating it is the concern of medical science (CCC 1673).

qa: Was the boy possessed or ill, perhaps with epilepsy?

The symptoms resemble epilepsy, and Matthew’s account uses a word often translated “epileptic” (Matthew 17:15). The Gospels present the case as the work of an unclean spirit. The Church is careful here: she believes in the reality of evil spirits, but she also insists that illness be treated by medicine and that exorcism be used only when there is moral certainty of possession (CCC 1673). In every case, Christ is the healer of the whole person.
study: Paul says that Christ became a curse for us so that we might receive the blessing. What “curse” in my life do I need to hand over to him?
The father said, “Look at my son.” For whom in my family do I need to pray with that simple trust this week?
